written.myAnswer: SI units are user friendly because they use powers of ten, making conversions straightforward. They are standardized and used internationally, which makes measurements easier to communicate and compare.
Other measurement systems include the CGS (centimetre–gram–second), MKS (metre–kilogram–second) and FPS (foot–pound–second) systems.
A metre is the SI unit of length. It is the distance travelled by light in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second.
SI units provide a common international standard, making it easier to communicate and compare scientific results. They also help scientists share data and reproduce experiments.
The five basic SI units commonly used in chemistry are metre (m) for length, kilogram (kg) for mass, second (s) for time, kelvin (K) for temperature and mole (mol) for amount of substance.

Area is measured in square metres (m²), volume in cubic metres (m³), and density in kilograms per cubic metre (kg m⁻³). These are derived units: area is length × length, volume is length × length × length, and density is mass divided by volume.
Chemical laboratory quantities are often small, so grams and cubic centimetres are more convenient to use than kilograms and cubic metres.
Different units make measurements harder to compare and understand. Converting between them takes time and can lead to confusion and errors.
Using standardized SI units avoids confusion and helps measurements be understood, compared and checked consistently. This reduces errors and supports reliable results and safe work.

SI units provide scientists and engineers worldwide with a common standard for measurements and data. This makes results easier to compare and share, reduces conversion errors and supports reliable collaboration in space exploration.
